newsitem.title: GREECE: GREECE TO HOLD BALKAN FOREIGN MINISTERS' MEETING.
newsitem.headline: GREECE TO HOLD BALKAN FOREIGN MINISTERS' MEETING.

text.p: Greece, concerned over instability at its northern borders, will hold a meeting of Balkan foreign ministers in June, Prime Minister Costas Simitis said on Tuesday.

Stressing the need for more coordinated action by the European Union and other international organisations to deal with crises in the volatile region, Simitis said Greece was taking a series of initiatives to help its neighbours.
"We are preparing a Balkan meeting at a foreign ministers level on June 9 and 10 in Salonika," he told a Balkan economic conference in this northern Greek city.

Simitis said the violent crisis in Albania, prompted by the collapse of pyramid investment schemes, and economic difficulties in Bulgaria showed that financial aid alone did nothing to solve long-term problems.

"Developments in Albania and Bulgaria showed that we need a more substantial policy from European institutions for the whole of the Balkans," he said. "Otherwise, any financial contribution would be throwing money down a bottomless pit."

Violence has gripped impoverished Albania as thousands left destitute after the collapse of the pyramid schemes raided army depots and plunged the tiny country into anarchy, roaming and looting at will.
Athens is also concerned there will be a new influx of refugees across its borders. Hundreds of thousands of illegal workers, mostly Albanians, are already taxing its straining economy.
Greece, whose businessmen have invested heavily in Albania and other Balkan countries, will extend a favourable loan to the tiny country as soon as stability is restored there, Simitis said.
Greek trade with the Balkans tripled between 1990 and 1995 and Greek exports have now risen to more than $1 billion a year, Simitis said.
But political stability and the development of democratic institutions were necessary for Balkan countries to develop, he added.

Athens was pushing through the EU a proposal that calls for the mobilisation of the European Commission, the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank and the European Investment Bank to aid Balkan countries in need.
"Greece's proposal aims at coping in the long-term with problems troubling countries at a transitional phase in our region," Simitis said.
